title: The transformations of mind (3.9–3.15)
hook: even stillness is a kind of change, and the same mark can mean one, ten or a hundred depending on where it stands

segments.voice: Yesterday: the three together, and your line, samyama. Concentration, meditation and absorption, braided on one thing. What did one full minute of looking show you? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

Write the number one on a piece of paper. A single upright stroke. Now put a zero after it. Same stroke, same ink, same paper, and it means ten. Add another zero. A hundred. The stroke didn't grow. Nothing about it changed, and yet everything about what it means changed, just by where it stands. The classical commentary on the Yoga Sutras uses this very example: one mark, worth one, ten or a hundred by its place. It's explaining today's sutras, about how things change, including the mind.
screen: `ONE STROKE OF A PEN.` → `ONE, TEN, A HUNDRED.` → `THE STROKE NEVER CHANGED.`

segments.voice: The word is parinama: transformation, change of form. Patanjali starts with the mind. Sutra 3.9: even stillness is a change. There's a moment when a scattering impression fades and a stilling impression rises, and the mind shifts toward quiet. Sutra 3.10: practiced again and again, that shift becomes a calm, steady flow. Then 3.11: scatteredness wanes, one-pointedness rises. And 3.12: the thought that fades and the thought that rises become alike, the same object, moment after moment. That's one-pointedness, described as a kind of change. Then he widens the lens. Sutra 3.13 says the same three changes run through everything, the elements and the senses too: change of property, change of time, change of condition. The commentary gives the stroke of the pen, and another picture: the same woman is called mother, daughter and sister, depending on who's speaking. Sutra 3.14 names what stays underneath: the substance that carries the properties, past, present and still to come. And 3.15: a different order produces a different change. The commentary's example is clay. A lump becomes a pot. The pot breaks into shards. The shards become dust. The clay is there the whole way through. Why put this in a book on meditation? Because if you're going to do samyama on anything, you need to see clearly what changes and what carries the change. And in the Yoga Sutras' wider picture, the seer itself doesn't change at all. Only the seen does.
screen: `PARINAMA: TRANSFORMATION.` · `EVEN STILLNESS IS A CHANGE.` · `MOTHER, DAUGHTER, SISTER.` · `CLAY: LUMP, POT, SHARDS, DUST.` · then, large: `WHAT CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice watches change happen in the mind. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Notice a thought arise, stay a moment and fade. Notice the next. Don't follow the stories. Just watch the shape: rising, staying, fading. Then notice the breath, also rising and fading. And notice what doesn't seem to rise and fade: the watching itself. Stay with that for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
The transformations of mind. Parinama, change of form: even stillness and one-pointedness are changes, carried by something that stays.
Your line: what changes. Today, notice one thing changing, coffee cooling, light moving across a wall, your own mood, and ask what's carrying the change. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 467 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KNOWLEDGE OF PAST AND FUTURE.`

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras study the transformations of 3.9–3.15 with the classical commentary, and in meditation practitioners watch thoughts arise and fade as a way of seeing change clearly.

pairs: one, ten or a hundred by place
stays through lump, pot and shards
the fading and rising thought alike

myth: Patanjali treats stillness as the absence of all change
3.9 describes stilling itself as a transformation of the mind.
the commentary explains change with a numeral's place value
one mark means one, ten or a hundred depending on its position.
in the Yoga Sutras' picture, the seer changes along with the mind
only the seen changes; the seer is unchanging.

fork.setup: you're holding a lump of clay. it becomes a pot, then breaks into shards. what has changed?
options: the form and stage; the clay is still there.
fork.reveal: the commentary's example: lump, pot, shards, dust. properties come and go; the substance that carries them stays (3.14–3.15).

original.note: Sanskrit pariṇāma: transformation, change of form; three kinds in 3.9–3.12 and three more in 3.13.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation stops the mind from changing.
what it means: stillness and focus are themselves changes, and everything changes in property, time and condition while the substance underneath remains.
what a scholar hears: nirodha-, samadhi- and ekagrata-parinama (3.9–3.12); dharma-, lakshana- and avastha-parinama (3.13); the Bhashya's numeral by place value and the clay.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 3.9–3.12 (the transformations of stilling, absorption and one-pointedness)
Yoga Sutra 3.13–3.15 (change of property, time and condition; the substance; sequence)
Yoga Bhashya on 3.13 and 3.15 (the numeral by place; mother, daughter, sister; clay)

notes: 'Some fifteen hundred years ago' for the Bhashya: dating is debated (often placed around the 4th–6th century CE); confirm or soften.
The place-value numeral example and the mother/daughter/sister example are attributed to the Bhashya on 3.13; confirm.
Clay example (lump, pot, shards, powder) attributed to the Bhashya on 3.15 (or 3.14); confirm.
